claims.text: The case reports acute leukaemia, bk virus infection, and cystitis haemorrhagic as reactions in a 13-year-old male receiving cyclosporine for graft versus host disease.
BK virus infection is listed in the cyclosporine label under warnings, with a specific mention of polyoma virus-associated nephropathy (PVAN) due to BK virus infection.
FAERS shows a strong disproportionality signal for cyclosporine and BK virus infection (PRR=94.173, ROR025=88.06, IC025=5.889), meeting Evans, ROR, and IC criteria.

Acute leukaemia and cystitis haemorrhagic are not found in the cyclosporine label and are not among the 80 most-reported reactions for cyclosporine in FAERS, so disproportionality is not available for these reactions.

The case includes multiple concomitant medications (e.g., fludarabine, cytarabine, methotrexate) that are known to be used in acute leukaemia and may confound attribution of acute leukaemia to cyclosporine.
The reflex judgment assesses causality as 'unassessable' due to confounding and limited information, despite a high seriousness probability (0.96).

memo.narrative: A 13-year-old male developed acute leukaemia, BK virus infection, and haemorrhagic cystitis while on cyclosporine for GVHD, with multiple concomitant leukemogenic and immunosuppressive drugs. BK virus infection is label-listed and shows a strong FAERS signal, but causality is unassessable due to confounding. The case is serious and requires expedited review.
open_questions: Whether acute leukaemia is disease-related or drug-induced cannot be determined from this case alone due to concomitant chemotherapy and underlying condition.
The role of cyclosporine in BK virus infection is biologically plausible and supported by label and signal, but individual causality remains unclear without temporal dechallenge/rechallenge data.

memo.narrative: A pediatric patient developed acute leukaemia, BK virus infection, and cystitis haemorrhagic while on cyclosporine for GVHD. BK virus infection is labeled and shows a strong FAERS signal. Acute leukaemia and cystitis haemorrhagic are not labeled and lack FAERS signals. Concomitant leukemogenic drugs (fludarabine, cytarabine) raise confounding by indication.
open_questions: Whether acute leukaemia represents disease progression or a new event, given concomitant fludarabine and cytarabine.
Whether cystitis haemorrhagic is related to cyclosporine, infection, or other comorbidities in this immunocompromised patient.

rules.text: Disproportionality (PRR, ROR, IC) shows a reporting association, never causation.
FAERS counts have no exposure denominator: no incidence, rate or risk estimates.
Do not rank or compare the safety of different drugs by disproportionality magnitude.
Absence of a disproportionality signal is not evidence of safety.
A reaction listed in the label does not confirm causality in this individual case.
A single case report cannot establish or confirm a signal on its own.
Number of PubMed hits is not a measure of evidence strength.
Counts may include duplicates and stimulated reporting; do not treat them as exact.
Confounding by indication and co-medication must not be ignored when attributing the reaction.
Model probabilities are population-calibrated, not certainty about this case.
No individual treatment advice or dosing recommendations for the patient.
Quoted label text must actually appear in the cited label section.
An evidence grade is population-level context: never cite the grade without its basis, and never as proof of causality in this case.
